ai.definition: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a method of securely distributing cryptographic keys using the principles of quantum mechanics to ensure that any attempt to intercept the key will be detected.
ai.howItWorks: QKD leverages the properties of quantum bits or qubits, which can exist in multiple states simultaneously. When these qubits are transmitted over a quantum channel (such as through photons), any eavesdropping would cause an observable disturbance due to the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle, ensuring the security of the key exchange.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the vulnerability of classical encryption methods that can be intercepted and potentially decrypted by adversaries without detection.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing QKD systems involves creating and manipulating single photons or other quantum particles in controlled environments. This process requires precise optical components, detectors, and complex electronics.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the quantum channel (e.g., fiber optic cables), generating qubits using lasers or other light sources, encoding information onto these qubits, transmitting them over the channel, and decoding at the receiver end while continuously monitoring for any disturbances that indicate eavesdropping.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the precision of photon generation and detection, complexity of quantum error correction algorithms, and the need for advanced optical components. High initial R&D investment also contributes to costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: expected growth as more applications are developed and regulatory frameworks mature
ai.regulation: Currently, there is no standardized global regulation for QKD, but efforts are underway to establish guidelines that ensure interoperability and security standards.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the need for stable quantum channels, susceptibility to environmental noise, and the complexity of integrating with existing communication infrastructure. Financial risks involve high initial costs and uncertain market adoption.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited due to high R&D costs and early stage commercialization. As technology matures and more applications are developed, profitability could increase.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving the efficiency of quantum key distribution, extending the distance over which keys can be securely exchanged, and integrating QKD with existing cybersecurity protocols.

glossary.def: A quantum bit that can exist in multiple states simultaneously, used for encoding information in QKD.

A fundamental concept in quantum mechanics stating that certain pairs of physical properties, like position and momentum, cannot both be precisely measured at the same time. This principle is exploited to ensure security in QKD.

subsystems.name: Transmitter
subsystems.role: prepares each bit as a faint laser pulse whose quantum state encodes 0 or 1.
parts: tuneable laser at telecom wavelength (about 1550 nm on fibre)
intensity modulator and attenuator down to single-photon level

subsystems.name: Quantum channel
subsystems.role: carries the photons without allowing them to be copied undetected.
parts: low-loss optical fibre, or a free-space/satellite link
optical amplifiers are avoided because they would copy the state

subsystems.name: Receiver
subsystems.role: measures each photon in a randomly chosen basis.
parts: single-photon avalanche diodes, or superconducting nanowire detectors needing cryogenic cooling

subsystems.name: Classical channel and authentication
subsystems.role: lets both ends compare notes publicly without leaking the key.
parts: pre-shared secret for the first handshake

subsystems.name: Post-processing
subsystems.role: turns raw detections into a short, secret key.

subsystems.name: Key management and integration
subsystems.role: delivers keys to the encryptors that actually protect traffic.

buildSteps.title: Generate raw bits
buildSteps.detail: A quantum random number generator produces the bit values and the measurement bases.

buildSteps.title: Encode and attenuate
buildSteps.detail: Each bit is written onto a laser pulse, then dimmed until pulses average less than one photon — in the BB84 scheme, four states in two incompatible bases.

buildSteps.title: Transmit
buildSteps.detail: Pulses travel through fibre as light, or through free space to a satellite, losing photons with distance.

buildSteps.title: Detect
buildSteps.detail: The receiver picks a random basis for each pulse; a click only counts when its basis matches the sender's.

buildSteps.title: Sift
buildSteps.detail: Over the ordinary network, the two sides announce which bases they used and keep only the coincidences.

buildSteps.title: Estimate the eavesdropper
buildSteps.detail: They measure the error rate. An intercepting attack raises errors, so a high rate means abort — this is the detection, not prevention, mechanism.

buildSteps.title: Correct and compress
buildSteps.detail: Error correction reconciles the two strings; privacy amplification hashes them into a shorter key about which an eavesdropper knows almost nothing.

buildSteps.title: Authenticate
buildSteps.detail: The classical messages must be authenticated, which requires a pre-shared secret — a bootstrapping weakness, not a quantum one.

buildSteps.title: Feed the encryptors
buildSteps.detail: Keys are stored and handed to one-time-pad or AES equipment, or relayed node by node across a network.

prerequisites.why: the whole scheme depends on counting individual photons; the best detectors need cryogenic cooling.

prerequisites.tech: Low-loss fibre or free-space optical links
prerequisites.why: photons cannot be amplified or copied, so distance is limited by loss alone.
without them, links beyond roughly a few hundred kilometres of fibre need 'trusted nodes' that hold the key in the clear.
QKD cannot authenticate itself; it needs a pre-shared secret or public-key signatures to start.
industry specifications and security evaluations exist but are still maturing, and real systems have been broken by implementation flaws such as detector blinding.
not a prerequisite, but a competing answer: software-only algorithms that resist quantum computers and need no new hardware.

pathway.milestone: metro and inter-city QKD links and national fibre backbones, plus financial-sector trials
pathway.unlocks: point-to-point key distribution between fixed sites at modest key rates.

pathway.milestone: chip-scale transmitters and receivers with trusted-node networks joining many cities
pathway.unlocks: lower cost and wider coverage, still with trusted relays at each node.

pathway.milestone: satellite key distribution for intercontinental links
pathway.unlocks: key exchange where no fibre exists, limited by weather and pass times.

pathway.milestone: quantum repeaters and entanglement distribution, eventually device-independent protocols
pathway.unlocks: genuinely long-range, relay-free security — the point at which the 'unbreakable' claim would hold broadly.
protection against future quantum computers for the many cases where new fibre and hardware are impractical.
